item.title: Menominee Nation elders are getting solar and battery systems
item.description:
Transcript:

In Wisconsin, the Menominee Nation is installing solar panels and battery systems at the homes of tribal elders.

Pyawasay: “Here on the reservation … with any major storms, we continuously lose power. And sometimes it’ll be for days, sometimes it’ll be for weeks, so we wanted to make sure that our elders were taken care of.”

That’s tribal utility director Darryl Pyawasay. The tribe is partnering with solar companies and nonprofit funders on the Elder Solar Program.

So far, he says they’ve installed solar and battery systems at the homes of about a dozen elders who need electricity to run medical equipment like dialysis machines or oxygen concentrators.

When the grid is down, the solar panels and batteries directly power their homes so people can get through an outage without disruption.

The rest of the time, energy from the solar panels flows back to the grid, reducing residents’ utility costs.

Pyawasay: “Most of our elders are on fixed incomes, and any way that we can help them save that money so they can put it towards groceries or put it towards gas … that was our priority.”

So the tribe is using clean energy to help some of its most vulnerable members save money and stay safe.

Reporting credit: Sarah Kennedy / ChavoBart Digital Media

item.title: Genevieve becomes the first Category 5 hurricane of 2026
item.description:
Intensifying at a dramatic pace, Hurricane Genevieve – which was nothing more than a tropical depression on Friday, July 24 – became the first Category 5 storm of 2026 in the Eastern Pacific at 5 a.m. EDT Monday, July 27, with top sustained winds touching 160 mph (257 km/hr) and a central pressure of 925 mb. As of 11 a.m. EDT Monday, Genevieve’s top sustained winds had dropped slightly to 155 mph (251 km/hr), which put the hurricane back in the Cat 4 range – albeit at the very top of that range. Genevieve is the first Eastern Pacific storm to hit Cat 5 status since Kristy in 2024.

Fortunately, Genevieve’s wrath is playing out far away from land. As of 11 a.m. EDT Monday, Genevieve was centered roughly 520 miles south-southwest of the southern tip of Baja California. Genevieve was moving northwest, roughly parallel to the Pacific coast of Mexico, at a brisk 14 mph. Steady steering currents are predicted to keep Genevieve well clear of any land areas over the next five days. The track is forecast to take a slight leftward bend over time, moving it even farther away from land.

Contributing to Genevieve’s rapid ascent to Cat 5 strength were light-to-moderate wind shear, a moist atmosphere (relative humidity above 80%), and sea surface temperatures of around 30 degrees Celsius (86 degrees Fahrenheit). The waters of the tropical Eastern Pacific from Genevieve west to the region south of Hawaii are experiencing near-record warmth for late July. This area lies just north of the Niño3.4 region that straddles the equator, where records for late-July oceanic warmth are getting pulverized – courtesy of the record-early onset of a powerful El Niño event.

As Genevieve took shape, it drew on a ribbon of exceptionally moist air extending from the Niño3.4 region, and this likely helped nurture the storm’s rapid growth.

Forecast for Genevieve

Genevieve is predicted to suffer the classic slow demise typical of powerful hurricanes moving west-northwest through the tropical Eastern Pacific. In this part of the world, hurricane-supportive oceanic warmth does not usually extend into the subtropics, as it often does in the western Atlantic. Sea surface temperatures beneath Genevieve’s path are predicted to drop below 25°C (77°F) by Thursday, falling below the standard 26°C threshold for hurricane sustenance. Genevieve will also be moving into increasingly dry air, with midlevel relative humidity dropping to around 50% by late week. Given these conditions, the NOAA/NWS National Hurricane Center predicts that Genevieve will steadily weaken, likely falling below hurricane strength by around Friday.

Genevieve is the planet’s fourth Category 5 tropical cyclone of 2026. The others to date:

  • Tropical Cyclone Horacio, 160 mph (260 km/h) winds, February 23, over the remote South Indian Ocean. Horacio did not affect any land areas.
  • Super Typhoon Sinlaku, 185 mph (295 km/hr) winds, April 12, southeast of Guam. Sinlaku made landfall over the U.S. Northern Mariana Islands on April 14, with the large eye of the storm passing over both Tinian and Saipan islands simultaneously. According to the Joint Typhoon Warning Center, Sinlaku was a Cat 4 with sustained winds of 145 mph (230 km/hr) at landfall. Sinlaku killed 17 and did about $1.5 billion in damage to the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam.
  • Super Typhoon Bavi, 180 mph (285 km/h) winds, July 5, a long-track typhoon over the northwest Pacific. Bavi struck the island of Rota in the U.S. Northern Mariana Islands at peak intensity, then weakened gradually before a second landfall near Zhejiang, China, on July 11, this time as a tropical storm. Damage of more than $140 million extended across a number of Northwest Pacific islands as well as parts of East Asia, and at least 23 people were killed. Bavi was the 11th Category 4 or 5 tropical cyclone to hit a U.S. state or territory in the past 10 years; that’s as many Cat 4 and Cat 5 landfalls as the U.S. Gulf and Atlantic coast suffered over the prior 60 years.

Squalls and swells from a weakening Fausto to affect northern and eastern Hawaii

Tracking well ahead of Genevieve, on a path that’s similar but displaced a bit farther south, Hurricane Fausto is en route to pass just north of the Hawaiian islands on Tuesday and Wednesday. Hurricane Fausto has continued moving quickly toward the west. It was officially named on July 19 and became a hurricane on July 20 over the warm waters of the Pacific Ocean. By Friday morning Hawaii Standard Time, Fausto reached Category 2 intensity, peaking with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (165 km/h).

Throughout last week, Fausto traveled over warm waters while maintaining a fairly symmetrical wind field. By Saturday, however, dry air began infiltrating the system. Fausto gradually weakened through Saturday and Sunday while maintaining its hurricane status. By Monday morning Eastern Time, Fausto was a Category 1 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 85 mph (140 km/h). The system continues moving west at about 15 mph (24 km/h).

As Fausto continues to weaken, it is forecast to be downgraded to a tropical storm as it encounters increasingly dry air and cooler sea surface temperatures. Current forecasts indicate that by Tuesday night into Wednesday morning local time, the center of Fausto should be just northeast of Honolulu, passing at a safe distance from the northern portion of the Hawaiian Islands. The latest forecast track from the National Hurricane Center shows that by Wednesday afternoon, the center of Fausto should pass about 80 miles (128 kilometers) north of Honolulu. Tropical-storm-force winds are predicted to extend only about 50 m (80 km) southward from Fausto by that point.

The primary factor contributing to Fausto’s weakening is the cooler sea surface temperatures. Fausto had been traveling over waters warmer than 80°F (27°C), but as of Monday, it is expected to move over waters closer to 77°F (25°C). These cooler waters will reduce the energy available to the hurricane, further weakening the system.

As with any tropical cyclone, the center of the storm could wobble over the next couple of days, leading to slight variations in its forecast track. In addition, increasing wind shear will continue to displace Fausto’s strongest thunderstorms and winds to the north of the storm’s center. This means the Hawaiian Islands should be spared from most of Fausto’s heavy showers and thunderstorm activity.

Nonetheless, despite the storm’s asymmetrical structure, the eastern and northern portions of the islands could still experience gusty winds and very high surf. East-facing shores are expected to see increasing seas, with surf potentially reaching high surf warning criteria between Monday night and early Wednesday. Some east-facing beaches could experience surf heights of 10 to 14 feet beginning Monday night.

By Tuesday night, as Fausto is forecast to move north of the islands, north-facing shores could see surf heights of 12 to 15 feet. Tropical Storm Warnings remain in effect for the open waters surrounding the entire Hawaiian island chain. However, the islands themselves are not under any tropical storm warnings or watches. High surf advisories and small craft advisories are in effect and will likely remain in place through the middle of the week.

As Fausto moves away, some rain bands may continue to move across the Hawaiian islands from east to west. If these rain bands linger over the same locations for an extended period, isolated flooding could occur in a few areas.

Watching Dolphin: Another Cat 5 storm could develop in the Pacific late this week

Far west of Hawaii, yet another tropical cyclone – newly named Tropical Storm Dolphin – is expected to become a formidable typhoon. Dolphin is predicted by the Joint Typhoon Warning Center to strengthen steadily over the next several days. In an unusually aggressive forecast late Sunday night, the center predicted Dolphin to reach Category 5 strength by late this week, as it moves amid light wind shear and favorable upper-level outflow over a part of the open northwest Pacific where sea surface temperatures are running 1-2°C (2–4°F) warmer than average. Dolphin is expected to avoid land areas, tracking well northeast of the U.S. Mariana Islands and south of Wake Island.

As for the Atlantic Ocean, no tropical cyclones of any consequence are expected over at least the next week, as hostile conditions typical of El Niño are ruling the roost.

Jeff Masters contributed to this post.

item.title: I saved more than $200 on my EV road trip
item.description:
When I received an invitation to my colleague Sam Harrington’s wedding, I was so honored. The Yale Climate Connections team had been through a pretty tough year of attacks on the free press and U.S. climate science, but we had made it through with laughter and tears. 

So I knew that I was absolutely showing up with my husband and 4-year-old for this wedding in Madison, Wisconsin, roughly 1,200 miles away from my home in Rhode Island. As with most things in my life, I procrastinated on booking airplane tickets and didn’t start to look at flights until a month or so out. I couldn’t find tickets under $1,300 for the three of us, so my husband and I started to talk about making the journey into a road trip. By that time, the Iran war had broken out, and gas prices were climbing.

After doing some math, we realized that our cheapest option was to take the Kia EV6 that I had leased in January. It seemed like it would be a fun experiment that I could also turn into an article for work, because why not make everything about work, am I right?

Turns out I was right: We saved over $200. 

Mapping out our route and hitting the road

My only real concern was whether there would be enough charging stations along the route. The longest trip I had done at that point in the EV was the 210 miles round trip between my house and Yale Climate Connections headquarters in New Haven, Connecticut. My husband and I did some rough mapping of the route to ensure that there were plenty of chargers in range and on our route, and it looked more than doable. We planned to make it to Wisconsin in two days, with an overnight stop somewhere in Ohio. We estimated we’d need to stop for about three charges each day. 

And so the adventure began! 

Trip to Wisconsin

  • Portsmouth, Rhode Island, to Elyria, Ohio: 655 miles and four charging stops
  • Elyria, Ohio, to Madison, Wisconsin: 488 miles and four charging stops

Our first charging stop was in Norwalk, Connecticut, at a Wegmans supermarket nearly 140 miles away from where we started. We weren’t super low on charge, but we had been in the car for a bit already and needed to use the restroom and (most importantly) eat lunch. After buying far too much food (which we do every time that we’re in Wegmans) and eating it, we set off on our merry way, fully charged in more ways than one. 

We stopped three more times that day. Although we honestly could have done it with just two more charges, I got a little bit of range anxiety in Pennsylvania when we were going through a rural part of the state. The Kia has a map of all the nearest chargers, so I didn’t even really need to plan anything out, but once we got down to 40%, I would start looking for charging stations. Much like in a modern gas car, the Kia also warned us once it got down to a certain range and suggested chargers that were nearby. 

I am not a fan of Elon Musk for many reasons, but it is difficult to get away from the fact that Tesla does seem to have the best charging infrastructure in the U.S. Their superchargers, or Level 3 chargers, are easy to find. My Kia is equipped with the Tesla charging port, making it easy and fast to charge up. Other options include:

  • EVgo also provides decent charging infrastructure, including superchargers. According to EVgo’s website, more than 40% of the U.S. population lives within 10 miles of an EVgo fast charger. 
  • PlugShare aggregates public charging stations all over the world. 

There are even apps that allow you to find private owners who have chargers that you can use. 

Charging my car from 10% to 80% took as little as 20 minutes on the superchargers, and with a 4-year-old in tow, by the time we went inside the rest area to go to the bathroom and buy a snack, we were already at 20 minutes. My husband said that it was nice to have those extra couple of minutes to slow down and stretch our legs. 

Each charge cost between $15 and $35, varying because of differences in sales tax and energy prices, the time of day, and, of course, how much charge we started with.

Return trip:

  • Madison, Wisconsin, to Cleveland, Ohio: 490 miles and three charging stops 
  • Cleveland, Ohio, to Portsmouth, Rhode Island: 628 miles and four charging stops

We charged our car for free at the hotel where we stayed in Madison. On our return trip, we took a northerly route and spent a night in Cleveland, Ohio, pulling into home in Rhode Island by 9 p.m. the following day. 

Pearl and Kai Marvell explore Madison, Wisconsin. (Image credits: Pearl Marvell)

We spent a total of $328.87 round trip to charge our EV. In comparison, if we’d driven my husband’s Toyota Tacoma hybrid instead, we would have spent between $500 and $600 on gas.

I would absolutely do an even longer road trip in an EV in the future. The ride was comfortable; EVs are super fun to drive, and it made me realize just how much infrastructure to support EVs is in place, despite the Trump administration’s efforts to kill clean technology. 

So, thanks, Sam, for getting married! Also, if you haven’t read her article about planning a climate-friendly wedding, you should.

item.title: People are mailing bloodthirsty ticks to a New York lab
item.description:
Transcript:

During the summer, stacks of envelopes arrive at a lab in upstate New York. Inside are ticks that people pulled off their bodies after spending time outside.

Thangamani: “And then we tell them what tick species it was, what life cycle stage it was, and what pathogen it carries.”

Saravanan Thangamani runs the Upstate Tick Testing Laboratory at SUNY Upstate Medical University.

He says tick populations are expanding in many parts of the Northeast, largely because of climate change.

As temperatures warm, ticks can survive in some areas that were once too cold for them and stay active longer in the year.

Climate change is also shifting the geographic range of some of the animals that ticks feed on.

Thangamani: “When this wildlife moves to a different geographic area, the ticks are carried along with them as well.”

Since 2019, his team has tested more than 30,000 ticks, mostly from New York.

They found that about a third carried one or more pathogens – like the bacteria that cause Lyme disease, the virus that causes tick-borne encephalitis, or the parasite that causes babesiosis.

So the lab gives people information they can share with their doctor, and it also gives scientists data to track the changing risks as the climate warms.

Reporting credit: Sarah Kennedy / ChavoBart Digital Media

item.title: Help us grow our bilingual coverage
item.description:
[Para leer en español, haga clic aquí]

¡Hola!

I became a meteorologist because I know that when a hurricane threatens, people in harm’s way need trustworthy, reliable, and practical information — right away. I joined the Yale Climate Connections team to help make that lifesaving information available to Spanish-speaking readers in the U.S., because too often, they can’t rely on local news for storm updates in their preferred language. 

In fact, more than 70% of our Spanish-speaking readers say that our coverage helps them stay safe during extreme weather. 

That’s why we’re asking readers like you to help us keep our extreme weather coverage going and growing. Will you become a donor today? 

Donate

As a bonus, every dollar you donate during this period will be matched, up to $10,000, thanks to generous support from an anonymous Yale Climate Connections reader.

To thank you for your support, if you become a monthly donor by August 1, you’ll be invited to join an exclusive, monthly-donors-only conversation with meteorologist Jeff Masters, Editor-in-Chief Sara Peach, and me over Zoom later this season. 

When you go to the donation page, make sure you’ve selected the “recurring” option, and remember that if you set up your donation to be anonymous, we won’t have your information to invite you to our Zoom conversation. August 1 is the last day to qualify.

If you’d rather donate by check, make it out to “Yale University” and write “For Yale Climate Connections” on the check. Mail it to: Yale Climate Connections, Yale University, Attn: Development Office, 205 Prospect Street, New Haven, CT 06511

Yale University is a nonprofit 501(c)3. Its federal tax ID is 06-0646973.

Donate

Thanks for your support as we prepare for peak hurricane season,

Irene Sans

item.title: The government canceled this nature study. Scientists kept going anyway.
item.description:
Most of us sense it without being told why: A walk in the woods or an hour in the park leaves us calmer, clearer, and restored. Increasingly, modern science agrees. A growing body of evidence links time in nature to better physical and mental health – and a major new effort is working to document exactly what that evidence shows.

That effort is called the Nature Record, and its survival is a story in itself. It began as the National Nature Assessment, a federal undertaking modeled on the long-running National Climate Assessment and mandated by a Biden-era executive order. Roughly 180 scientists volunteered to develop about a dozen chapters. The project had reached an early public-comment draft when the Trump administration canceled it. Rather than abandon the work, the authors decided to finish it independently under a new name, with foundation funding and National Academy of Sciences review. The report is now under revision, with the final release slated for December 2026.* 

Howard Frumkin, a physician-epidemiologist and a professor emeritus at the University of Washington, led the assessment’s chapter on human health. Yale Climate Connections spoke with him about how the report survived, what the science says about nature’s health benefits, why those benefits aren’t shared equally, and what it all means for communities and the healthcare system.

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Yale Climate Connections: The connection between nature, health, and climate change pulls together fields that don’t usually sit at the same table. How do you frame that intersection?

Howard Frumkin: This intersection of the natural world and human health – in the context of climate change – draws on three different lineages intellectually.

The first is the scientific evidence on the health benefits of nature contact, which is what the Nature Record is focusing on. So if you or I take a walk in a forest or in a park, we have nature contact, and something about that is good for us. We don’t fully understand. It might be the visual appreciation of beautiful nature; it might be phytoncides – biogenic chemicals that we’re inhaling. It could be the quiet, could be the physical activity. But nature also delivers benefits without direct contact: The upstream ecosystem in the watershed that delivers clean water is good for health. We may never go up there, but we still benefit from it.

The second is the whole literature on climate solutions, indicating that coastal mangrove forests and sponge cities and tree canopy deliver benefits both in terms of climate mitigation and adaptation: We can store carbon, reduce temperatures of neighborhoods, we can manage storm water.

Then there’s a third line of thinking, which has to do with the human relationship with the natural world. In Indigenous and tribal wisdom, there’s talk of reciprocity, the shared relationship that we have as part of nature, the obligations for stewardship, the legal concepts of the rights of nature. All of that is related to, but different than, the climate benefits piece because it’s explicitly not instrumental; it’s not transactional; it’s relational. You come into that thinking about the right relationship that we as humans should have with the natural world – not because of what it gets us.

Yale Climate Connections: So how did the Nature Record come to be, and how did the project survive after the federal government withdrew its support?

Frumkin: It was a pretty simple concept: the idea that you can’t take good care of what you don’t know. There was a perception that if we were to be good stewards of our natural heritage in this country, we needed an inventory. We needed to take stock of what we had, and not just at a fixed moment in time but over time to understand the trends that were affecting nature and the benefits it delivers. The model for doing that was the National Climate Assessment, which is the every-four-year assessment of climate change in the U.S. – how it’s unfolding, what the impacts are on humans – mandated by federal legislation back in the 1990s. It comes with lots of federal procedures, in terms of scientific rigor, transparency, public review, and so on. Out of that conceptual commitment to taking stock of what we have, and using the model of the National Climate Assessment, an executive order in the Biden administration mandated the creation of the National Nature [Assessment].

It got as far as a “zero order draft,” – what regular people call an outline – that was published in the Federal Record and made available for public comment. And no sooner did that happen than the Trump inauguration happened, and the Trump administration killed the National Nature Assessment.

By then we had rostered around 12 chapters with around 15 authors each, so we had 180 authors all volunteering time, representing academic institutions and agencies and NGOs across the country. And pretty much in the blink of an eye, everybody said, “Let’s do it anyway … This work is so important, and the value is so clear that we don’t need to be a federal undertaking.”

There were some legal issues, like we couldn’t use the same name; federal employees could no longer participate because of potential risks to them and to the project. We found foundation support in early 2025, and by mid-2025 [it was] clear that we had enough money, energy, and commitment that we could continue. We landed on the Nature Record, and we’re proceeding almost in some ways as if it were a federal document – with transparency, National Academy of Sciences review, very careful documentation of all factual claims – partly because rigor will give a lot of credibility to the report, and partly because it would be a good thing for this to return to being a federal effort. If we have followed all the rules, dotted all the i’s, and crossed all the t’s, this can be reimported into government.

That said, being nonfederal offers some advantages. We can be more flexible and nimble, more creative in the ways we undertake outreach and build partnerships, and publicize and disseminate what we find. In some ways, this is a blessing in disguise. We have, for example, a national poetry effort running alongside the Nature Record, and we’ve published a book of poetry. We’ve engaged young people in graphic arts related to the benefits of nature. Bringing that creativity to bear has been a really nice part of the project.

Yale Climate Connections: When you dug into the evidence for the health chapter, what were the biggest takeaways or trends you saw?

Frumkin: The first key message is that, in general, nature contact is good for people; it’s health-promoting. The second is that those benefits are unequally distributed across society. Some of us have much better or easier access to nature than others. It’s an equity issue, because poor people and people of color disproportionately tend to have less access to parks and high-quality park programming, through the legacies of redlining and other historical trends.

But it’s not just that conventional form of equity that’s important. People with disabilities have difficulty accessing natural places. Older people have difficulty because too many parks lack accessible trails and shade, and children often lack access because safe, easy access to green space is rare in many communities.

Another trend is more screen time and less green time. People are spending less time outdoors. On the other hand, there are some emerging technologies that may facilitate nature contact, such as Merlin [the birdsong identification app], which may help deepen people’s appreciation of nature, and there’s reason to think that being more familiar with it deepens nature connectedness.

Four takeaways about health and nature from the Nature Record

  • Nature contact is broadly good for human health.
  • Those benefits are unequally distributed – by race, income, age, and disability.
  • Long-term trends, such as rising screen time and falling green time, are reshaping how people benefit – for better and worse.
  • Evidence-based interventions, like well-designed park programming, can reliably strengthen nature’s health benefits.

Yale Climate Connections: If the evidence that nature helps is solid, how much do we actually know about why – and about how much nature is enough?

Frumkin: One of the most interesting parts of this is that although we have pretty solid evidence that nature contact benefits health, we know precious little about how it works. So you may walk through a forest and benefit from seeing the natural beauty of the forest. We have lab evidence that T cells do better after contact with natural compounds than they otherwise would. It may be that the benefit comes from the fact that you’re walking through the forest with friends, and social contacts in natural settings are soothing and restorative. It may be that natural settings call on us just to get out there and take a walk, and the physical activity is a really effective promoter of good health.

Not knowing the pathways and mechanisms of benefits makes it a little difficult to prescribe. And we don’t know a lot about the varieties of nature and which ones are more or less effective. Do you need trees, or do shrubs do the trick? Do you need immersion, or viewing nature out the window? Do you need the real thing, or might virtual nature provide some of the same benefits? Do you need to get out every day, or does a few times a week suffice? So these are a lot of questions we still need to try to answer.

The potential benefits of nature contact are strong, much less expensive than pharmaceuticals, free of side effects, and don’t need to be prescribed by a licensed healthcare provider. The cost-benefit implications are potentially enormous if we get it right and understand best how to optimize those benefits.

Yale Climate Connections: As a physician, I hear a real fear of nature from patients: ticks and mosquito-borne disease, allergies, wildfire smoke, and extreme weather – and climate change is heightening those risks. How do you balance nature’s benefits against these threats?

Frumkin: Rarely in life can you eliminate risk altogether, but you can manage risk.

The risks of being outside: Well, there’s a risk of sunburn – but we can manage that risk with sunblock and with protective clothing. The risk of ticks – that’s a real risk. But we can manage that risk: inspecting ourselves after we’ve been in tick-infested areas and using bug repellent to keep the ticks away. So for each risk, we can reduce the risk by managing it well.

Yale Climate Connections: How do you hope communities will use the Nature Record?

Frumkin: So for communities, here’s an example. Almost every community in the country now has a housing shortage, and there is a need to build more housing. And to do that in economically and environmentally efficient ways generally means density. Density can collide with protecting nature. This report will make it clear that balancing the protection of nature with fulfillment of other human needs – like housing – is a key set of trade-offs we need to tackle and be explicit about.

Using the insights from this report, design strategies that both protect nature and provide nearby nature contact and also provide housing and transportation – which means in many cases nonmotorized transportation, active transport, cycling, and walking. The design of communities needs to take into account all these needs: environment, human, and equity.

Yale Climate Connections: Hospitals and health systems have a natural connection to health, not only through the care they provide but also through the spaces they create. As they consider land use decisions, including parking needs and opportunities for green space, what should they keep in mind?

Frumkin: Two thoughts. One is that we know a lot about how to build green, and that means the buildings themselves, with biophilic principles. It means the environmental performance of the buildings – what are called green buildings – and it means the situation of buildings in lots, protecting nearby nature. That’s a good way to build; it’s economical. There may be increased up-front costs, but they’re generally recoverable in a short number of years, and they deliver health benefits to patients and staff.

The second message is that nonprofit hospitals are required to carry out community health needs assessments and to invest in community health based on the findings of those assessments.

Nature deficit is a community health need, and in my view ought to be a part of every community health needs assessment. To the extent that it’s documented, hospitals can consider investing funds in local parks, either for developing parks or planning programming in parks that we know improve community health.

I would urge hospitals to think about nature deficit as one of those community health needs and then consider investments in nature contact for people in their catchment areas as a means of promoting public health.

Yale Climate Connections: Finally, what makes you most hopeful?

Frumkin: For me, one of the biggest potential sources of despair is the polarization and ideological hysteria that seems to be sweeping our country and many others as well. But this topic offers a counterbalance, because across the political spectrum people love the natural world and appreciate it.

Hunters and anglers and campers may be far right politically, but they have common cause with environmentalists who may be on the political left. There aren’t too many domains that can unite us across the ideological divide that bedevils the country now, but this is one.

I think the fact that we’re approaching this entire Nature Record in an apolitical way, and framing it in terms of benefits that all Americans can enjoy, gives me hope that we may be able to help overcome one of the biggest challenges we face.

*Editor’s note: This article was updated July 27, 2026, to clarify that the final report has not been released.

item.title: An old Atlanta railway is becoming a cool escape
item.description:
Transcript:

In Atlanta, an overgrown and neglected railroad corridor is becoming a shady walking and biking path.

When complete, the Atlanta Beltline will form a 22-mile loop around the city, linking parks, affordable housing, art, businesses, and public transit.

And hundreds of different types of plants and trees will surround the path – forming the world’s longest linear arboretum.

Levine: “And it’s a way that people can get through 45 neighborhoods, either by bike or by foot, that is going to be completely shaded.”

Greg Levine is executive director of the nonprofit Trees Atlanta, which manages the arboretum.

He says the design incorporates both old-growth trees and new tree plantings.

As climate change causes more extreme weather, these trees will help keep the city cool on hot days. And they’ll filter stormwater when it rains.

They’ll also create habitat for wildlife.

Levine: “In the evenings, you can hear insects. … If you get there early in the morning, there’s birds flying all around.”

More than half of the arboretum has already been built.

And signs, artwork, and docent-led tours on the path teach people about the trees and the ecosystem as they enjoy the winding oasis of greenery.

Reporting credit: Ethan Freedman / ChavoBart Digital Media

item.title: Help us cover hurricanes; become a sustaining donor
item.description:
Hi everyone,

One of the most rewarding things about working in meteorology is that our work can actually save lives. Since 2020, my colleague Jeff Masters and I have provided critical coverage of some of the most severe weather events of the century at Yale Climate Connections. Our stories have been read and shared by tens of thousands of people in the paths of tropical cyclones, including hurricanes and typhoons — in Florida, in the Caribbean, and around the world. In the U.S. and Caribbean, this decade’s hurricanes have cost nearly $400 billion and taken more than 1,600 lives.

This year, Jeff and I are thrilled to be joined by our new meteorologist, Irene Sans, who is helping us expand our Spanish-language coverage of hurricanes. We want to make this our most successful season of hurricane reporting to date, and that’s why we’re asking for your help today.

Through the end of this month, we’re running a reader fundraising drive to help us ensure that we can continue to grow our work to help people protect themselves and their loved ones during extreme weather. And thanks to a generous Yale Climate Connections reader, every dollar you donate by August 1 will be matched, up to $10,000. 

“Yale Climate Connections provides essential help with hurricane planning for this lifelong Floridian,” a reader told us. “As heat, drought, rain, flooding and more change how we live, I expect to rely on Yale Climate Connections even more.”

We’re hoping to add 50 new monthly donors before the end of the month. Will you help us?

Donate

If you join as a monthly donor during this fundraising campaign, you’ll be invited to join an exclusive conversation with Jeff Masters, Irene Sans, and Editor-in-Chief Sara Peach over Zoom later this season. 

One-time donations are meaningful, too. We aren’t funded directly by Yale University, so donors of all types are essential to keep our work going. Every bit of support makes a difference!

When you go to the donation page, make sure you’ve selected the “recurring” option, and remember that if you set up your donation to be anonymous, we won’t have your information to invite you to our Zoom conversation. 

If you’d rather donate by check, make it out to “Yale University” and write “For Yale Climate Connections” on the check. Mail it to: Yale Climate Connections, Yale University, Attn: Development Office, 205 Prospect Street, New Haven, CT 06511

Yale University is a nonprofit 501(c)3. Its federal tax ID is 06-0646973.

Donate

Thanks for your support as we prepare for peak hurricane season.

item.title: Simple tweaks can make wastewater treatment less polluting
item.description:
Transcript:

Wastewater treatment plants remove pollutants from sewage before it returns to lakes, rivers, and oceans.

But that treatment process can produce some harmful pollution of its own.

Jose Porro is CEO of Cobalt Water Global, a company that helps water utilities reduce their nitrous oxide emissions. Nitrous oxide is a powerful global warming gas.

Porro: “Nitrous oxide is also an ozone-depleting gas.”

And it can be created as an unintended byproduct of wastewater treatment, during the removal of nitrogen.

Nitrogen is present in people’s urine and has to be removed because if it ends up in waterways, it can cause harmful algae growth and other problems.

But under certain conditions, the microbes that break down nitrogen can produce nitrous oxide.

Porro says the problem can often be fixed through simple tweaks – for example, aerating the water less at certain times so less oxygen gets in.

So his company uses machine learning to help utilities monitor and fine-tune their processes.

Porro: “We’ve been able to achieve up to 80 to 90% reductions in the N2O emissions from making simple process adjustments.”

So water treatment plants can clean the water – without adding as much pollution to the atmosphere.

Reporting credit: Sarah Kennedy / ChavoBart Digital Media

item.title: Tropical Storm Bertha makes its second U.S. landfall, degenerates into a trough
item.description:
Update (Thursday, July 23, 11:00 p.m. EDT):

Tropical Storm Bertha became history during the 11:00 p.m. EDT advisory on Thursday evening. The tropical storm made landfall a second time in the United States, this time near the Texas-Louisiana border on Thursday afternoon. This came after its first landfall in St. Bernard Parish, Louisiana, on Wednesday afternoon.

The storm traveled slowly throughout Thursday, moving mainly to the west-northwest. During the latter part of the afternoon, it began to accelerate, with its forward speed surpassing 10 mph. On satellite imagery, it was difficult to determine the exact location of the center, as it appeared to hug the Louisiana coastline throughout the day. However, the second landfall was officially declared because the center of its center of the storm had moved completely inland, which is the criterion required for an official landfall.

The cluster of storms that had been displaced by wind shear began to move onto the central Texas coast during the late afternoon and evening hours, bringing periods of showers to coastal southeast Texas. Overall, southeast Texas remained mostly quiet under mostly cloudy skies, with occasional gusty winds. The strongest winds were observed along the coast, where isolated power outages and a few downed tree limbs were reported. Overall, impacts along the Gulf Coast — from Louisiana through Texas — were minimal. Along the central Texas coast, rainfall totals generally ranged from one to two inches, with minor flooding reported, especially in poor-drainage areas. However, these are conditions that can be typical during summer afternoons. The more significant impacts were observed over the coastal waters, where high surf, a high risk of rip currents, and minor storm surge occurred.

Let this storm serve as a lesson: Every storm IS different

It is important to remember that every storm is different. Bertha produced minimal impacts largely because wind shear displaced its convection and kept the strongest thunderstorms over the open waters of the Gulf, also preventing it from strengthening further. This was an atypical storm, with several factors working against its development but ultimately benefiting those along the Gulf Coast. Residents should not use this storm as a reference for any future system that may impact the area. Remember, every storm is unique, and the atmospheric conditions surrounding a storm can either exacerbate its impacts or, as happened with Bertha, significantly reduce them.

Update (Wednesday, July 22, 3:30 p.m. EDT):

Tropical Storm Bertha has officially made landfall near the Biloxi Wildlife Management Area in St. Bernard Parish, Louisiana, around 2 p.m. CDT, as announced in a special statement put out by the NHC. Bertha is about 40 miles east of New Orleans and continues to move west-northwest at 7 mph (11 km/h). Gusty winds are expected to increase along the warned areas.

Original article, posted on Wednesday, July 22:

Tropical Storm Bertha is approaching the southeastern coast of Louisiana as it moves slowly west-northwest. The 2 p.m. EDT Wednesday, July 22, advisory indicated that Bertha holds maximum sustained winds of 45 mph (75 km/h).

Tropical Storm Warnings are in effect for the metropolitan New Orleans area and the Lake Pontchartrain region. You can expect tropical storm conditions, meaning winds that could exceed 39 mph, to remain in place at least through the overnight hours Wednesday into Thursday. It is likely that the Tropical Storm Watches that are in effect across the central and western coast of Louisiana will be upgraded to Tropical Storm Warnings during the next advisories.

Keep in mind that Bertha, although it’s expected to increase its forward speed a little, will continue to move slower than average, at under 10 mph, through the next two days. This will be an all-week event as the system continues to brush the Louisiana coast throughout Wednesday and into early Thursday.

Hurricane Hunters indicated that Bertha’s center of circulation could be weakening, and it is possible that a new center of circulation could form closer to the cluster of thunderstorms that has been shifted mainly over water. So as Bertha continues to move slowly west and its center emerges over water, it will likely remain a tropical storm and not completely dissipate. However, it will be battered by wind shear, which means that Bertha is not likely to intensify before arriving in Texas near Galveston, likely on Thursday afternoon.

Once Bertha makes landfall, it will be the second storm this season to form and to make landfall in the Gulf Coast. Arthur made landfall on June 17 in southern Louisiana, bringing torrential rains that may have set a new all-time 24-hour precipitation record for the state: 29.06 inches (738 millimeters) near Cottonport, Louisiana. According to Gallagher Re, Arthur is responsible for at least $1 billion in damage and four deaths.

An unusual storm

Bertha has demonstrated that it’s not a typical tropical storm. With a strong high-pressure system to the north and very strong wind shear coming in from the north-northeast, much of the convection, which runs in the troposphere between 6,500 and 16,000 feet (2,000 and 5,000 meters) high, has been shifted over the open waters of the Gulf. Yes, there have been some rain showers and thunderstorms pushing across Florida and the Southeast, but these have been intermittent.

The biggest issue with Bertha has been the gusty winds that have brought very rough surf conditions and storm surge along the immediate coast. Panama City Beach recorded a sustained wind of 42 mph on Tuesday, and gusts above 50 mph were recorded along the Panhandle Coast. Storm surge will likely produce flooding along the immediate Gulf Coast east of the storm center; up to three feet of storm surge is possible, especially when the winds and location coincide with high tide.

The latest satellite image shows some breaks in the clouds across the Florida Panhandle, with the deepest convection moving slightly ahead of the system but still to the southwest of the center and over the Gulf. The winds are coming in directly from the south across the western portion of Florida through the Mississippi and Alabama border as the system’s center crosses southeastern Louisiana.

Central Texas Coast will likely be most impacted by Bertha’s rain

The heaviest cluster of thunderstorms associated with Bertha, which has been shifted well south of the center of the storm, will likely impact the central coast of Texas, extending from areas just south of Galveston County through the Corpus Christi area on Thursday afternoon and evening. Expect rainfall along the immediate central coast of Texas to range between two and four inches, while the greater Houston area will likely receive less than an inch of rain.

As far as the winds, they will remain around tropical storm strength across the central and western coast of Louisiana through Thursday afternoon. As the system moves closer to southeast Texas, the winds will start to diminish across Louisiana and likely pick up across the Galveston Bay area later Thursday afternoon as the system’s center approaches. The system will quickly dissipate as it moves over the Lone Star State.

It is quite rare for the first two named storms of the season to make a U.S. landfall. The last time this occurred was also during a strong El Niño year, 2015:

· Tropical Storm Ana (May 10): Made landfall near Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, becoming the earliest U.S. tropical cyclone landfall on record at the time.

· Tropical Storm Bill (June 16): Made landfall along the Texas coast near Port O’Connor.

Over the past 30 years, the U.S. has averaged just over three landfalls by named storms per year, with two of those landfalls being from hurricanes.

Has Bertha brought dangerous heat to the South?

Over 55 million people are under some sort of heat advisory across the U.S., but the highest concentration is over the South Central and Deep South. Bertha has ignited some interesting contrasts in warnings along the Gulf Coast on Wednesday. As our colleague Michael Lowry highlighted on his Substack Wednesday morning, it is very unusual to see heat advisories and extreme heat warnings in effect over the same areas that are being impacted by a tropical storm and are also under tropical storm warnings. This clearly shows how different Bertha has been from a typical tropical storm.

We have seen this mixture of warnings because strong wind shear has kept the deepest convection well away from the center and to the south. In most other situations, a tropical storm would bring a broader, deeper layer of clouds, which would keep temperatures below the threshold needed to trigger heat alerts. But with Bertha, the strong wind shear shifting that thick cloud layer away from land has allowed temperatures to soar. Heat index values could rise as high as 115°F through 7 p.m. CDT Wednesday across many areas of the Deep South. The heat alerts extend widely across the Deep South and westward over more than half of eastern Texas, reaching as far north as southern Oklahoma. A frontal boundary extends from the Appalachians through Arkansas and into southern Oklahoma, keeping all of the heat bottled up from Mississippi westward through much of Texas.

Read: The emerging danger of post-hurricane heat waves

Is there anything else brewing in the Atlantic basin?

Aside from Tropical Storm Bertha, the National Hurricane Center does not have anything else highlighted across the Atlantic basin for the next seven days.

The latest satellite imagery shows two tropical waves emerging from Africa, one ahead of the Cabo Verde Islands and another deeper cluster of thunderstorms just southeast of the Cabo Verde Islands. However, these systems are not likely to develop within the next seven days. The rest of the central and western Atlantic continues to be dominated by Saharan dust, which will bring hazy skies across Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic, Haiti, and eastern Cuba over the weekend.

Eastern Pacific stays active, but no immediate threats to land

Of the two named storms in the Atlantic plus six in the Eastern Pacific this season, just one has made it to hurricane strength thus far: Hurricane Fausto, which is currently churning through the remote Northeast Pacific between Mexico and Hawaii after reaching Category 1 strength on Monday evening, July 20. That’s a full three weeks later than the average arrival date of the first Eastern Pacific hurricane, even though the region is running several weeks ahead of schedule on named storms.

As of 11 a.m. EDT Wednesday, Fausto was centered about 850 miles west-southwest of Cabo San Lucas, Mexico, moving west-northwest at 7 mph (11 km/h) with top sustained winds of 80 mph (130 km/h). Fausto’s pulsing central core of showers and thunderstorms (convection) was accompanied by a broader shield of convection extending well to the east. Wind shear is moderate (10 knots), and sea surface temperatures along Fausto’s path are just 1 degree Celsius above the typical hurricane-sustaining threshold of 26°C (79°F),  so Fausto appears likely to maintain its strength over several days and could intensify slightly at times. However, NHC was not predicting Fausto to reach Category 2 before it encounters gradually cooler waters and a steadily drier atmosphere. The latter will bring midlevel relative humidity down from about 75% on Wednesday to around 50% by the coming weekend.

The model consensus is for Fausto to pass just north of the Hawaiian Islands early next week as a weakening tropical storm, though some models – including some members of the Google DeepMind ensemble, the top performer on Atlantic tropical cyclone tracks in 2025 – suggest Fausto or its remnants could pass directly over the islands.

Jeff Masters and Bob Henson contributed to this post.
